Deadlock Isn't a Dead End: Using the Buy-Sell to Force Price Discovery

A well-built shotgun clause turns stalemate into a number. When owners deadlock, a buy-sell that forces one side to name a price at which it will either buy or sell breaks the impasse by making price discovery unavoidable — while a badly built one hands the leverage to whoever moves first or has the deeper pockets.
A well-built shotgun clause turns stalemate into a number. A badly built one hands the leverage to whoever moves first.

Deadlock is the failure of a two-owner company to make a decision it needs to make. Left alone, it destroys value — the business drifts while the owners fight, and a court-ordered dissolution sells the enterprise at the worst possible time. A properly drafted buy-sell is the private alternative, and its job is to force a price when the owners cannot agree on one.

The classic mechanism is the shotgun, or Texas, clause. One owner names a single price. The other must either buy at that price or sell at it. The discipline is elegant: the naming party cannot lowball, because it may be forced to sell at its own number, and cannot inflate, because it may be forced to buy. In theory, self-interest produces a fair price.

In practice, the clause rewards asymmetry. An owner with far greater liquidity can name a price the other cannot afford to match, forcing a sale below true value. The fix is structural — financing periods, installment terms, or an appraisal floor that keeps the mechanism from becoming a wealth transfer to the richer owner.

The lesson is that the buy-sell is not boilerplate. Drafted with attention to who holds the money and who holds the leverage, it turns deadlock into orderly price discovery. Drafted carelessly, it becomes the weapon the stronger owner uses on the weaker one.

Exit Readiness: The Three Value Gaps Owners Discover Too Late

Owner dependence, customer concentration, and undocumented process quietly cap the multiple a buyer will pay — and owners usually discover them only in diligence, when it is too late to fix. Closed years before a sale rather than months, each of the three converts personal value into transferable enterprise value the market will actually pay for.
Owner dependence, customer concentration, and undocumented process quietly cap the multiple. Close them years before the sale, not months.

Most owners assume the business is worth what it earns times a multiple, and the multiple is roughly fixed. It is not. The multiple is a measure of how risky and how transferable the earnings are, and three recurring gaps push it down — often without the owner noticing until a buyer's diligence team names them.

The first is owner dependence. When the relationships, decisions, and technical knowledge run through one person, the buyer is buying that person, not the company. A management layer, delegated authority, and documented decision rights convert owner value into enterprise value.

The second is customer concentration. A business where one or two accounts drive much of the revenue carries a risk the buyer prices heavily, because the loss of a single relationship can impair the whole investment. Diversifying the base, and locking in the anchor accounts with real contracts, narrows the gap.

The third is undocumented process. When how the business runs lives in habit rather than in systems, the buyer cannot be confident the earnings survive the transition. Written processes, clean financials, and transferable systems make the earnings look durable — which is what a higher multiple actually rewards.

None of the three closes in the ninety days before a sale. They close over years, which is why exit readiness is a planning discipline, not a transaction task.

When the IRS Challenges Your Gift-Tax Valuation: Building a Record That Holds

The appraisal that survives examination is built before the gift, not after the notice. A defensible gift-tax valuation is a contemporaneous, qualified appraisal that documents its assumptions, discounts, and methodology at the transfer date — so that when the IRS challenges the number, the record answers the challenge instead of inviting it.
The appraisal that survives examination is built before the gift, not after the notice. What a defensible file looks like.

Gift-tax valuation is where aggressive planning meets a motivated examiner. Owners transfer minority interests in a family entity, apply discounts for lack of control and marketability, and report a value well below the pro-rata share of the underlying assets. The discounts are legitimate. Whether they hold depends almost entirely on the quality of the record built at the time of the gift.

A defensible file starts with a qualified appraisal by an independent, credentialed appraiser, prepared contemporaneously with the transfer. It states the standard of value, identifies the interest transferred, and supports each discount with data — restricted-stock and closed-end-fund studies for marketability, control-premium evidence for the minority discount — rather than a rule of thumb. It reflects the actual terms of the operating agreement that create the lack of control and marketability in the first place.

The weak file is assembled after the notice of examination. It reads as reverse-engineered to a predetermined answer, and examiners and courts treat it accordingly. Adequate-disclosure rules matter too: a properly disclosed gift starts the statute of limitations, and a poorly disclosed one leaves the valuation open for years.

The through-line is timing. Discounts win when the appraisal, the entity documents, and the disclosure were all in place before the gift. They lose when the planning outran the paper.

How Key-Man Discounts Actually Work When Fixing the Value of a Business

When one person is the business, a key-man discount is real — but it is never automatic, and the other side will fight its size. It sticks only when the record shows that the enterprise's earnings genuinely depend on a single owner and that the dependence cannot be cured at reasonable cost.
When one person is the business, the discount is real — but it is not automatic, and the other side will fight its size. Here is what makes it stick.

A key-man discount reflects a simple risk: if the business would lose material value on the departure, disability, or death of one individual, a buyer pays less for it. The appraiser quantifies that risk and reduces value accordingly. The concept is sound. The fight is always about magnitude.

The discount sticks when the dependence is documented and structural. Revenue concentrated in relationships the key person owns personally. Technical or licensing capability that lives in one head. Customer loyalty that follows the individual, not the entity. Where those facts are on the record, a discount in the range appraisers actually apply is defensible.

It fails when it is asserted rather than shown, or when the dependence is curable. A management team in place, transferable customer contracts, documented processes, an earn-out or employment agreement that retains the key person through transition — each of these shrinks the discount, because each reduces the risk the buyer is being asked to bear.

For the owner arguing for the discount, the work is to prove the business cannot be easily separated from the person. For the owner arguing against it, the work is to prove it can. Either way, the number turns on evidence, not on the label.

The Owners Never Signed Post-Employment Restrictions. What That Does to Value.

A departing owner who can compete tomorrow is a discount the buyer will demand today. When the owners never signed non-competition or non-solicitation covenants, the missing protection shows up directly in the number — because a buyer cannot pay full price for goodwill that can walk out the door and set up across the street.
A departing owner who can compete tomorrow is a discount the buyer will demand today. The missing covenant shows up in the number.

Goodwill is what a buyer pays for above the value of the hard assets. In a closely held company, much of that goodwill is personal — it lives in the owners' relationships, reputations, and know-how. Restrictive covenants are what convert personal goodwill into enterprise goodwill the buyer can actually own. Without them, the conversion is incomplete.

In a buyout, the continuing owner is the buyer, and the departing owner is free to compete. That freedom is not academic. It is a live risk that the customers, referral sources, and employees the business depends on will follow the departing owner out. A rational buyer prices that risk, and the price is a reduction in value.

This is where the absence of planning becomes a valuation event. Had the covenants been signed at formation, the goodwill would transfer cleanly. Because they were not, the appraiser confronts a genuine question about how much of the enterprise's value is durable in the departing owner's absence.

The lesson runs in two directions. In a live dispute, the party positioned to compete holds leverage the valuation must account for. In planning, covenants signed at the beginning — when everyone is friendly and no one is leaving — are among the cheapest value protection an owner will ever buy.

# Fair Value vs. Fair Market Value: The Discount Fight That Decides the Case

Fair market value prices the block of stock. Fair value prices a proportionate share of the enterprise. Between those two definitions sits thirty to fifty percent of the money, and the question is usually settled — by statute, by contract, or by default — before either expert opens a workbook.

Lawyers treat the standard of value as a preliminary. It is not. It is the case. An expert given the wrong standard produces a competent report answering a question nobody asked, and the error is often invisible until cross-examination, because the arithmetic underneath is identical either way. Same normalized earnings, same multiple, same discount rate. The divergence happens in the last two lines.

## Three standards, and what each one is for

Fair market value is the Revenue Ruling 59-60 construct: the price at which property would change hands between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither under compulsion, both reasonably informed. Both parties are hypothetical. Because they are hypothetical, they have no particular reason to want this company, and the thing being priced is the specific interest as it sits in the holder's hands — which means a twenty percent membership interest with no control, no exit, and no market gets priced accordingly. This is the standard for gift and estate tax, for most buy-sell formulas that use the term, and for anything the IRS reviews.

Investment value is value to an identified holder, including that holder's financing, tax position, and synergies. It is the standard a strategic acquirer actually uses. It appears in litigation mostly as an argument about what the fair value number should look like.

Fair value is a statutory term that the statutes creating it decline to define. It governs the court-ordered buyout under N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7(8), the New Jersey appraisal remedy under N.J.S.A. 14A:11-1 to -11, the New York elective buyout under Business Corporation Law § 1118, and Delaware appraisal under 8 Del. C. § 262. Its content is judge-made, and the content that matters is this: the object of the valuation is the company, not the shares.

Delaware said it plainly in *Cavalier Oil Corp. v. Harnett*, 564 A.2d 1137 (Del. 1989). The appraisal values the corporation itself rather than a fraction of its shares as they exist in a particular shareholder's hands, and the shareholder receives his proportionate interest in a going concern. Discounting the individual holding, the court wrote, penalizes the minority for lack of control and hands the majority a windfall. New York reached the same place in *Friedman v. Beway Realty Corp.*, 87 N.Y.2d 161 (1995).

The practical consequence is that a minority discount has no place in a fair value determination in any of these jurisdictions. That is not a close question. What remains genuinely contested is marketability.

## New Jersey: equitable, not categorical

New Jersey decided *Balsamides v. Protameen Chemicals, Inc.*, 160 N.J. 352 (1999), and *Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith*, 160 N.J. 383 (1999), on the same day, and they point in opposite directions on the facts while resting on a single principle.

In *Lawson Mardon Wheaton*, dissenting shareholders were bought out and the company applied a twenty-five percent marketability discount. The Supreme Court held the discount inapplicable absent extraordinary circumstances, reasoning that applying it would enrich the majority, penalize minority holders for invoking the appraisal statute, and encourage squeeze-outs.

In *Balsamides*, the oppressed shareholder was the buyer rather than the seller. A discount was applied — because refusing to apply it would have let the oppressor extract full undiscounted value on his way out the door.

The principle uniting them is that a marketability discount cannot be used unfairly by the controlling or oppressing shareholder to benefit himself at the expense of the minority. New Jersey asks who is buying, who is selling, and who caused the buyout. That is an equitable inquiry, and it is genuinely more flexible than New York's categorical rule.

Flexible cuts both ways, and *Wisniewski v. Walsh*, 2015 N.J. Super. Unpub. LEXIS 3001 (App. Div. Dec. 24, 2015), shows the edge of it. A twenty-year family trucking dispute produced a twenty-five percent marketability discount applied against a selling shareholder whose conduct had driven the litigation. The valuation community reacted badly and with reason: nothing about the marketability of a trucking company changes based on how a shareholder behaved. The discount was doing equitable work under an economic label. Whether or not that is sound policy, it is the law you have to advise around, and it means a New Jersey fair value outcome depends on facts an appraiser cannot model.

## The agreement usually wins

None of the above matters if the parties wrote something down.

*Namerow v. PediatriCare Associates, LLC*, 461 N.J. Super. 133 (Ch. Div. 2018), is the case to read before arguing about standards. A retiring physician sought a fair market valuation of the practice. The operating agreement specified a net worth methodology, keyed to the last value the members had agreed on, adjusted for changes in net worth — and the members had not updated the number in years. The court enforced the agreement as written. Sixteen years of contrary course of conduct did not modify it, and a breach of fiduciary duty claim could not be used to obtain a valuation methodology the plaintiff had not bargained for.

That is the ordinary result. A buy-sell provision naming a standard, a formula, or an appraisal process displaces the statutory default for the transaction it covers. The statutory fair value framework governs when there is no agreement, when the agreement does not reach the triggering event, or when a court finds the mechanism inadequate.

Which makes the drafting question the whole ballgame, and most agreements get it wrong in a specific way: they say "fair market value" because it sounds neutral and it is the phrase the accountant used. In a two-member company where the departing member's interest is being bought by the only other member, fair market value with discounts prices a control transfer as though it were a sale of a minority stub to a stranger. The buyer captures the discount. Nobody intended that at signing, and by the time it matters, nobody can renegotiate it.

## The matrimonial divergence

Matrimonial valuation in New Jersey runs on a similar rule and different logic, which is why matrimonial and business divorce numbers on the same company can properly differ.

*Brown v. Brown*, 348 N.J. Super. 466 (App. Div. 2002), applied the extraordinary circumstances standard outside the oppression context, and *Denike v. Cupo*, 394 N.J. Super. 357 (App. Div. 2007), restated the operative reason: discounts are generally inapplicable where there is no actual transfer of shares and no likely sale of the business. In equitable distribution the interest is not being sold. It is being counted. A discount for the difficulty of selling something nobody is selling is a fiction.

Goodwill is where the real divergence lives. *Dugan v. Dugan*, 92 N.J. 423 (1983), defined goodwill as reputation likely to generate future business and made professional practice goodwill distributable — but the value has to be goodwill that survives the practitioner and transfers to a successor. That inquiry, personal versus enterprise, drives more variance between two competent appraisals of a professional practice than every discount argument combined.

## What to do about it

Plead the standard. In an oppression complaint, say that fair value governs and cite the statute. Do not let the case reach expert reports with the standard unresolved, because at that point one side has spent forty thousand dollars answering the wrong question and will fight to keep the answer.

Instruct the expert in writing. The engagement letter should state the standard of value, the valuation date, the premise, and whether discounts are to be considered and on what authority. This document gets produced. Written badly, it is the first exhibit on cross. Written well, it frames the expert's opinion before opposing counsel gets to.

Read the agreement before you theorize about the statute. If there is a functioning buy-sell covering the triggering event, *Namerow* is the likely outcome and the litigation is about whether the mechanism was triggered, not what the company is worth.

Fight marketability on economics, not on equity, if you can. A discount defended by comparable data and restricted stock studies survives appeal. A discount defended by how badly the other side behaved is available in New Jersey, but it is discretionary, unpublished, and it will not travel to another jurisdiction.

The standard of value is not a technical preliminary that the experts will sort out. It is the first substantive ruling in the case, and in most closely held buyouts it is worth more than everything argued after it.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the difference between fair value and fair market value?**
Fair market value prices the specific interest as it exists in the owner's hands, between hypothetical parties, and therefore accommodates minority and marketability discounts. Fair value prices the enterprise as a going concern and awards the owner a proportionate share of it. The same company can produce numbers thirty to fifty percent apart depending on which standard applies.

**Does New Jersey allow marketability discounts in a fair value buyout?**
Only in extraordinary circumstances. *Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith*, 160 N.J. 383 (1999), and *Balsamides v. Protameen Chemicals, Inc.*, 160 N.J. 352 (1999), hold that a marketability discount cannot be used by a controlling or oppressing shareholder to benefit himself at the minority's expense. Whether the circumstances are extraordinary turns on who is buying, who is selling, and who caused the buyout.

**Can our operating agreement override the statutory standard?**
Usually yes, for the transactions the agreement covers. *Namerow v. PediatriCare Associates, LLC*, 461 N.J. Super. 133 (Ch. Div. 2018), enforced a net worth valuation clause as written notwithstanding sixteen years of contrary practice, and rejected an attempt to reach a different methodology through a fiduciary duty claim.

**Why is the number in my divorce different from the number in my partner dispute?**
Different standards and different premises. In equitable distribution no interest changes hands, so discounts for illiquidity are generally inapplicable, and the personal-versus-enterprise goodwill question under *Dugan v. Dugan*, 92 N.J. 423 (1983), removes value from a professional practice that a buyout analysis might include.

**Who decides which standard applies?**
The court, on the statute and the agreement — but in practice the parties frame it. The standard should be pleaded and stated in the expert engagement letter before any appraisal work begins.

# Strategic Buyer or Hypothetical Buyer: Who Sets Fair Value in a Buyout?

Fair value is not fair market value. It measures the enterprise as a going concern, not the price a minority block would fetch from a stranger. That distinction opens the door to the strategic buyer, the acquirer who pays more because the company is worth more inside his own. Whether a court walks through the door depends on the record.

A minority member of a New Jersey limited liability company was offered a number for his interest. It was built the way these numbers are usually built. Normalized earnings, a multiple drawn from small-company transactions, a haircut for lack of control, another for lack of marketability. The majority presented it as arithmetic.

The arithmetic missed something. The company held a position a larger competitor needed and could not build quickly. Once that competitor entered the case as a documented fact — a named party, under a nondisclosure agreement, with the balance sheet to close — the argument stopped being about multiples of a small company's earnings. The interest sold for roughly twice the opening number.

Nothing about the company had changed. What changed was the identity of the buyer standing in the room.

## What a strategic buyer actually is

A financial buyer underwrites the business standing alone. He models the cash flow, prices the risk, assumes an exit multiple, and solves for a return. He will not pay for anything he cannot get from the company as he finds it.

A strategic buyer underwrites the combination. He is buying what the target adds to assets he already owns: a distribution channel, a licensed capability, capacity in a constrained market, a customer relationship that took a decade to earn, or the removal of the competitor who has been holding down his pricing. The benefits accrue on his income statement, not the seller's, and they will never appear on the seller's statements while the seller owns the company. That is the whole point. The seller cannot capture them. The buyer can, and will pay a share of them to get them.

Valuation calls that increment synergy. Lawyers should call it what it is in a dispute: the difference between what the majority wants the court to value and what the enterprise is worth to the market that wants it.

## Three standards, and the one most people conflate

Fair market value is the price at which property would change hands between a hypothetical willing buyer and a hypothetical willing seller, neither under compulsion, both reasonably informed. That is the Revenue Ruling 59-60 construct, and its hypothetical buyer is deliberately impersonal. He is no one in particular, which means he has no synergies, because synergies belong to someone in particular.

Investment value is the opposite. It is value to an identified owner, with that owner's synergies, financing, and tax position included.

Fair value is neither. It is a creature of statute, undefined in the statutes that use it, and its content comes from the case law. In New Jersey it governs the court-ordered buyout under N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7(8) and the appraisal remedy under N.J.S.A. 14A:11-1 to -11. In New York it governs the elective buyout under Business Corporation Law § 1118. In Delaware it governs appraisal under 8 Del. C. § 262.

The common error, made by lawyers and by more valuation analysts than should be making it, is to treat fair value as fair market value with the discounts stripped out. It is not. Delaware settled the unit of valuation in *Cavalier Oil Corp. v. Harnett*, 564 A.2d 1137 (Del. 1989): the object is the shareholder's proportionate interest in a going concern, and the task, in the Vice Chancellor's formulation that the Supreme Court endorsed, is to value the corporation itself rather than a specific fraction of its shares as they exist in the hands of a particular shareholder. New Jersey and New York run the same way. *Balsamides v. Protameen Chemicals, Inc.*, 160 N.J. 352 (1999); *Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith*, 160 N.J. 383 (1999); *Friedman v. Beway Realty Corp.*, 87 N.Y.2d 161 (1995).

That is the opening. Once the thing being valued is the enterprise rather than the block, the hypothetical buyer of fair market value theory has no work left to do, and the live question becomes the one the majority least wants asked. Worth as a going concern to whom?

## The doctrine that cuts the other way

Take the counterargument seriously, because opposing counsel will make it and some of it is right.

Delaware's appraisal statute directs the court to determine fair value "exclusive of any element of value arising from the accomplishment or expectation of the merger." 8 Del. C. § 262(h). The Delaware Supreme Court has read that as a command to find "the going concern value of the company irrespective of the synergies involved in a merger." *M.P.M. Enterprises, Inc. v. Gilbert*, 731 A.2d 790, 797 (Del. 1999). *Cavalier Oil* itself instructs that the company be valued as an operating entity without regard to post-merger events or other possible business combinations. 564 A.2d at 1145. The exclusion from consideration of post-merger synergies is a hard-and-fast rule in Delaware's jurisprudence.

Read carelessly, that is fatal to the strategic buyer argument. Read correctly, it is narrower than it looks, and *Verition Partners Master Fund Ltd. v. Aruba Networks, Inc.*, 210 A.3d 128 (Del. 2019), shows why. The court there fixed fair value at $19.10 per share, the price Hewlett-Packard paid less the synergies HP expected from the combination, and reversed the Court of Chancery for using the unaffected trading price instead. The court did not ignore the strategic acquirer. It started with the strategic acquirer's price and subtracted the piece the acquirer itself created.

The exclusion is transaction-specific. It removes value that the acquirer manufactures by combining, in the very deal under review. It does not hold that a company's attractiveness to acquirers is irrelevant to what the company is worth. Those are different propositions, and the distinction is the hinge of the whole argument: synergies created by the transaction are excluded, while the demand latent in the enterprise, available to a class of buyers, is a fact about the company on the valuation date.

## New Jersey's opening

New Jersey never adopted § 262(h)'s exclusion, and its fair value jurisprudence is expressly equitable rather than formulaic. Two features matter.

The first is *Lawson Mardon Wheaton*. The valuation date was December 5, 1991. Four and a half years later, Alusuisse-Lonza acquired the company at $63 per share. The trial court refused to reopen the record, reasoning that the acquisition price was neither known nor knowable at the valuation date. The Supreme Court reversed, remanding "after reopening the record for the limited purpose of considering the significance of the $63.00 per share Alusuisse merger price." Read the holding precisely. The merger price did not become fair value. It became admissible evidence against which the court's number could be tested, notwithstanding that it postdated the valuation date by years and involved a strategic acquirer. A New Jersey court that excludes a real acquisition price from a fair value proceeding is out of step with its own Supreme Court.

The second is the statute. The purchase price in a court-ordered buyout is fair value "as of the date of the commencement of the action or such earlier or later date deemed equitable by the court, plus or minus any adjustments deemed equitable by the court." N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7(8)(a). The valuation date is a variable, not a constant, and so is the number that comes out of it. For limited liability companies, N.J.S.A. 42:2C-48(a)(5)(b) permits relief where controlling members act oppressively to the applicant's harm, and § 48(b) authorizes the court to order "a remedy other than dissolution," with the listed remedies expressly non-exhaustive. That is a wide grant.

## The market approach already concedes the point

There is a quieter version of this argument that is easier to win because the other side usually makes it for you.

The guideline transaction method values a company off completed acquisitions of comparable businesses. Most acquisitions of privately held operating companies are made by strategic buyers, and the transaction databases record the prices actually paid. Nobody strips the synergies out before the multiple goes into the study. Any expert who applies a transaction multiple has already imported strategic pricing into his own conclusion.

The fight then is not about the standard of value. It is about comparable selection: whether the transactions chosen reflect the buyer universe that actually exists for this company, or a set of smaller, unrelated deals selected because they produce a lower multiple. That is a much better fight. It is an evidentiary argument about the expert's work, made on the expert's own chosen method, and it does not require the court to adopt any novel proposition of law.

## Where the leverage actually comes from

Everything above concerns what a judge might find. The more valuable insight is that the judge's number is the fallback, not the deal.

A buyout is an option, and an option is priced against the alternative. The majority's alternative is not "pay whatever the court decides." It is "live through the process that produces that decision, with the company's fate uncertain while it runs." In a corporation the majority can shorten that exposure. New York's § 1118 election cuts off dissolution and converts the case into a valuation proceeding fixed as of the day before the petition was filed. New Jersey's § 14A:12-7(8) motion works similarly.

New Jersey's LLC statute contains no equivalent entitlement. The court may order a buyout as a remedy other than dissolution, but the majority cannot elect one as of right, and the alternative remedy sitting on the other side of the ledger is a court-supervised disposition of the business. If a strategic buyer is standing there with a checkbook, that disposition is not a liquidation at distressed prices. It is an auction the majority might lose, or might win only by outbidding the party who values the company most.

That is the mechanism. The strategic buyer does not persuade the majority that fair value is higher. He changes what the majority is buying. The purchase is no longer a minority interest priced off an earnings multiple; it is continued control of an asset that somebody else wants. Reservation prices move a long way when the question changes from what will the judge say to what does control cost.

## The buyer who does not exist will be used against you

In the AriZona Beverages buyout, the largest of its kind in New York, the petitioner pointed to expressions of interest from potential acquirers. The court rejected the comparable analyses, relied solely on a discounted cash flow, and then treated the failure of those expressions of interest to ripen into bona fide offers as evidence of illiquidity supporting a 25% marketability discount. *Ferolito v. AriZona Beverages USA LLC*, 2014 N.Y. Slip Op. 32830(U) (Sup. Ct. Nassau Cnty. Oct. 14, 2014).

The lesson is not that strategic interest is inadmissible. It is that unconsummated interest proves the opposite of what its proponent intends. A buyer who kicked tires and walked away is affirmative evidence that the company is hard to sell.

So the standard is exacting. Named party. Written proposal. Financial capacity to close, demonstrable. Nondisclosure agreement and real diligence access. Corroboration from the transaction record showing that the sector is consolidating and who has been buying. A broker's teaser and a warm phone call will not survive cross-examination, and worse, they will be turned into a discount.

## Sequencing, and what breaks in practice

Surface the buyer before the valuation date. In New York that date is fixed the day before the petition is filed, and in New Jersey it defaults to the commencement of the action. *Lawson Mardon Wheaton* shows that later evidence can still get in, but no case should be built on winning that fight.

Read the transfer restrictions before making the first call. A right of first refusal that lets the majority match at a formula price converts your strategic bid into a subsidized acquisition of your own client's interest.

Route the contact through counsel and under a nondisclosure agreement. A minority member who shops the company on his own invites claims for breach of the operating agreement's confidentiality provisions, breach of fiduciary duty, and interference. Where the exposure is real, seek the court's authorization for a limited market check before running one.

Expect the counter-move. A sophisticated majority responds to a credible bidder by moving immediately for a buyout election to fix the valuation date and convert the matter into an appraisal, where the strategic buyer becomes at most an evidentiary exhibit. Whoever controls the timing controls a good part of the value. Move first.

And do not overreach. A price that depends on synergies unique to one acquirer invites the Delaware answer, and some version of that answer is available to any court that wants it. Build the case on a class of buyers with a common reason to want the company. Demand from a market is a fact about the enterprise. Demand from one man is an anecdote.

Fair value is a legal construct, but it is decided by people looking at evidence drawn from the real world. The record that wins is the one that makes the strategic buyer a fact about the company rather than an argument about the case.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is fair value the same as fair market value?**
No. Fair market value assumes a hypothetical willing buyer and seller and prices the specific interest being transferred. Fair value in a statutory buyout or appraisal values the enterprise as a going concern and awards the owner a proportionate share of it. The difference routinely exceeds the entire amount in dispute over discounts.

**Can a court consider an offer from a strategic buyer in setting fair value?**
In New Jersey, yes. The Supreme Court in *Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith*, 160 N.J. 383 (1999), required the trial court to reopen the record to consider an actual acquisition price that postdated the valuation date by more than four years. The offer is evidence to be weighed, not a substitute for the court's determination.

**Does fair value include synergies?**
Not the synergies created by the transaction under review. Delaware's appraisal statute excludes value arising from the accomplishment or expectation of the merger, 8 Del. C. § 262(h), and *M.P.M. Enterprises, Inc. v. Gilbert*, 731 A.2d 790 (Del. 1999), enforces that exclusion. Demand for the company from a class of acquirers is different: it is a market fact about the enterprise on the valuation date, and it reaches the number through the market approach in any event.

**What does this mean for the value of my LLC interest?**
It can mean a materially higher price, but only if the buyer is real and appears early. Documented interest from a funded acquirer changes what the majority is deciding, because the alternative to buying you out is a sale process the majority may not win. Expressions of interest that never become offers can cut the other way and support a marketability discount.

**When does the strategic buyer have to surface?**
Before the valuation date, and before the majority elects a buyout. Interest that appears after the case is framed as a valuation proceeding reads as litigation-driven and invites a known-or-knowable objection you may win but should not need to.

Fair value in a statutory buyout or appraisal values the enterprise as a going concern and awards the owner a proportionate share of it. The difference routinely exceeds the entire amount in dispute over discounts.

Can a court consider an offer from a strategic buyer in setting fair value? In New Jersey, yes. The Supreme Court in Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith, 160 N.J. 383 (1999), required the trial court to reopen the record to consider an actual acquisition price that postdated the valuation date by more than four years. The offer is evidence to be weighed, not a substitute for the court’s determination.

Does fair value include synergies? Not the synergies created by the transaction under review. Delaware’s appraisal statute excludes value arising from the accomplishment or expectation of the merger, 8 Del. C. § 262(h), and M.P.M. Enterprises, Inc. v. Gilbert, 731 A.2d 790 (Del. 1999), enforces that exclusion. Demand for the company from a class of acquirers is different: it is a market fact about the enterprise on the valuation date, and it reaches the number through the market approach in any event.

What does this mean for the value of my LLC interest? It can mean a materially higher price, but only if the buyer is real and appears early. Documented interest from a funded acquirer changes what the majority is deciding, because the alternative to buying you out is a sale process the majority may not win. Expressions of interest that never become offers can cut the other way and support a marketability discount.

When does the strategic buyer have to surface? Before the valuation date, and before the majority elects a buyout. Interest that appears after the case is framed as a valuation proceeding reads as litigation-driven and invites a known-or-knowable objection you may win but should not need to.

A marketability discount may be applied in an oppression buyout when equity requires it. Where the oppressor is the seller and the oppressed shareholder is the buyer, applying the discount prevents the oppressor from receiving a windfall and recognizes the illiquidity the buyer will bear.
Justia (public case text; not an issuing-court archive)

Two equal owners of a closely held chemical distributor could no longer operate the company together, and the trial court ordered the oppressing owner to sell to the oppressed owner. The Supreme Court upheld a marketability discount because requiring the buyer to pay an undiscounted price would reward the seller whose conduct caused the remedy and leave the buyer to absorb the company's illiquidity on a later sale.

The Court distinguished fair value from fair market value and separated a minority discount, which reflects lack of control, from a marketability discount, which reflects lack of liquidity. The decision does not establish an automatic discount. It makes the equities of the particular buyout—especially who is buying, who is selling, and whose conduct caused the remedy—central to the analysis. Read with *Lawson Mardon Wheaton*, it shows why similar valuation terminology can produce different outcomes when the parties' positions are reversed.

Appraisal values the corporation as an operating entity and awards the dissenter a proportionate interest in that going concern; a shareholder-level minority or marketability discount is improper.

Harnett held a small minority interest, and the corporation argued that appraisal should reflect the price at which that particular block could be sold. The Delaware Supreme Court rejected the premise. Appraisal first values the corporation as a going concern and then allocates the dissenter's proportionate share. Applying a minority or marketability discount at the shareholder level would penalize the dissenter and transfer value to the remaining shareholders or acquirer.

The opinion also defines an important boundary for acquisition evidence. The enterprise is valued as it existed at the merger date, without value attributable to post-merger events or other possible business combinations. The case therefore supports enterprise-level valuation while cautioning against importing value created only by a particular transaction or buyer.

In valuing an interest in the AriZona beverage enterprise, the trial court relied principally on a DCF analysis, declined to treat unconsummated expressions of interest as reliable transaction value, and applied a 25% marketability discount based on multiple company-specific illiquidity risks.
New York State Law Reporting Bureau

The dispute required the court to value an ownership interest in the closely held AriZona beverage business. The court used a discounted-cash-flow framework and declined to adopt preliminary expressions of acquisition interest as transaction value because they never matured into bona fide offers and did not establish what a buyer would actually pay on the valuation date.

The court applied a 25% discount for lack of marketability. Its conclusion rested on a collection of company-specific risks, including transfer restrictions, pending litigation, the absence of audited financial statements, tax uncertainty, and the limited reliability of prior indications of interest. The decision is an unreported trial-level ruling. It is useful as a fact-intensive example, but it should not be reduced to a rule that failed buyer interest alone determines the discount.

Goodwill is reputation likely to generate future business, and the goodwill of a professional practice is subject to equitable distribution where it has value as a going concern beyond the practitioner's personal earning capacity.

*Dugan* is filed under matrimonial law and belongs in every business divorce practitioner's working set, because it draws the line that determines how much of a professional practice is worth anything at all. Goodwill is reputation likely to generate future business. The distributable portion is the goodwill that exists as a going concern independent of the individual — value a successor could buy and keep.

That distinction, personal goodwill against enterprise goodwill, does the work that key-person discounts are usually asked to do, and it does it at the right point in the analysis. A key-person discount reduces the value of an asset the entity owns, and it invites the response that the person is not actually leaving. A personal goodwill argument says the value was never the entity's to begin with. Absent an enforceable covenant not to compete, the practitioner takes it with him.

The practical consequence in a single-rainmaker firm is large enough to swallow the discount fight entirely. Two competent appraisers who agree on every multiple, every rate, and every normalization adjustment will still be far apart if one treats the founder's client relationships as institutional and the other treats them as personal. Establish which they are — through referral source documentation, contract assignability, and what happened when other producers left — before arguing about percentages.

Fair value measures a dissenting shareholder's proportionate interest in the value of the enterprise. A discount based on the shares' minority status may not be applied.

Minority shareholders dissented from transactions involving family-owned real-estate corporations. The corporations' expert valued the interests from net asset value and then applied an adjustment that cross-examination revealed to be a minority discount. The Court of Appeals upheld elimination of that discount.

New York fair value gives the minority its proportionate share of enterprise value rather than the hypothetical trading price of a powerless block. The rule against a minority discount is categorical and avoids transferring value from the dissenter to those who remain. The opinion should not be cited for the broader proposition that every marketability discount is forbidden; New York law treats minority status and lack of marketability as distinct valuation questions.

The New Jersey appraisal statute gives qualifying dissenting shareholders a procedure to demand payment of the fair value of their shares following specified corporate actions, with judicial appraisal available when the parties do not agree on value.

Chapter 11 provides New Jersey's procedural appraisal remedy. It identifies the corporate actions that trigger dissenters' rights, prescribes notice and demand requirements, and provides for an offer by the corporation followed, when necessary, by a court proceeding to determine fair value.

The statutory phrase does not resolve every valuation issue by itself. New Jersey decisions, including *Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith*, explain that fair value protects the dissenter's proportionate interest in the enterprise and ordinarily does not permit a marketability discount that would transfer value to the majority. The statutory procedure and the judicial interpretation should therefore be read together.

An unambiguous operating agreement valuation provision is enforced as written. Sixteen years of contrary practice did not modify it, and a fiduciary duty claim could not be used to obtain a valuation methodology the member had not bargained for.

A pediatric practice's operating agreement said that if the members failed to agree on a new company valuation for more than two years, the buyout price would be built off the last agreed value, adjusted for changes in net worth. The members signed a Certificate of Agreed Value at $2.4 million on January 1, 2000, and never signed another one. Dr. Namerow announced his retirement in 2016 — the first retirement in the practice's history, and the first occasion to apply a provision nobody had thought about in sixteen years.

He argued that the periodic fair market value appraisals the members had obtained over the years for planning and settlement purposes established a course of conduct that modified the agreement, and that enforcing the stale certificate breached fiduciary duties owed to him. Neither worked. Where a contract is unambiguous the court will not look outside the four corners to determine intent, and parol evidence will not alter plain meaning. The oppression and fiduciary duty claims were dismissed on summary judgment.

This is the case to read before theorizing about statutory fair value, because a functioning buy-sell displaces the statutory default for the transaction it covers. It is a Chancery Division decision and therefore persuasive rather than binding, but it is published and it is cited regularly for the four-corners rule.

The drafting lesson is worth more than the holding. Nobody at signing intended a valuation frozen at the millennium. The clause failed not because it was unfair but because it contained no consequence for the thing the members were most likely to do, which was nothing. Any agreement keyed to a periodically certified value needs a stated fallback for the years when the certificate does not get signed.

Merger price and prior offers may be relevant in appraisal, but the Court of Chancery may give them no weight when the proponent fails to connect them to the company's going-concern value rather than buyer-specific or merger-created synergies.

In a statutory appraisal following M.P.M.'s sale to an industrial buyer, the corporation argued that the Court of Chancery had to give weight to the merger terms and two earlier offers. The Delaware Supreme Court affirmed a DCF-based appraisal that assigned those transactions no weight. Although arm's-length market values can be reliable evidence, the proponent had not established a nexus between the offers and M.P.M.'s going-concern value at the merger date.

The opinion draws the line directly: section 262 values the company to the stockholder as a going concern, not to a third party as an acquisition, and excludes merger-created synergies. A buyer-side DCF designed to give all synergies to the seller was therefore impermissible. *M.P.M.* is a material limitation on any claim that the strategic buyer itself defines Delaware fair value.

Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith

A marketability discount ordinarily should not be applied in determining the fair value of dissenting shareholders' stock absent extraordinary circumstances. A later arm's-length acquisition price may be considered as evidence of value even when it postdates the valuation date by several years.

The corporation restructured in a manner that triggered dissenters' rights and then sought to purchase the dissenters' stock with a discount for lack of marketability. The Supreme Court held that such a discount is ordinarily unavailable absent extraordinary circumstances because it would penalize the dissenters, benefit the controlling owners, and encourage squeeze-outs.

The Court also directed the trial court to reopen the record to consider a merger price paid approximately four and one-half years after the valuation date. The later transaction did not automatically establish fair value. It was potentially probative evidence whose significance had to be assessed on remand. The distinction matters: *Lawson* permits real transaction evidence to test an appraisal, but it does not hold that every strategic acquisition price—or any buyer-specific synergy embedded in it—equals statutory fair value.

N.J.S.A. 42:2C-48 — Judicial Dissolution and Alternative Remedies

A court may dissolve a New Jersey limited liability company on statutory grounds including unlawful or impracticable operations and oppressive conduct directly harmful to a member, or order another remedy—including a sale of a member's interest—when that relief is fair and equitable.

Section 42:2C-48 governs judicial dissolution and alternative relief for New Jersey limited liability companies. On application by a member, the statutory grounds include unlawful operations, impracticability of carrying on the company's activities in conformity with its formation documents, and conduct by controlling members or managers that is illegal, fraudulent, or oppressive and directly harmful to the applicant.

The court may order a remedy other than dissolution when that remedy is fair and equitable, including the sale of the applicant's interest to the company or other members. Unlike the corporate buyout provision, the LLC section does not provide a detailed valuation formula or an automatic election to purchase. The operating agreement, the nature of the wrong, and the court's equitable remedial choice remain important to any valuation analysis.

After a qualifying dissolution petition, the corporation or other shareholders may make an irrevocable election to purchase the petitioner's shares at fair value, ordinarily measured as of the day before the petition was filed and without value created by the filing itself.

Section 1118 permits the corporation or one or more shareholders to elect to purchase the shares of a shareholder who has petitioned for dissolution under specified provisions of the Business Corporation Law. The election ordinarily must be made within ninety days after the petition is filed and, once made, is irrevocable unless the court allows withdrawal on equitable terms.

If the parties cannot agree, the court stays the dissolution proceeding and determines fair value as of the day before the petition was filed, excluding any value arising from the filing itself. The election converts a dissolution dispute into a compulsory valuation proceeding, but the statute does not make the petitioner's shares equivalent to a freely marketed minority block. *Friedman v. Beway Realty Corp.* supplies the controlling rule against minority discounts.

When market quotations are unavailable, the fair market value of closely held stock is determined from all available financial data and all relevant factors under the hypothetical willing-buyer and willing-seller standard; no single formula controls.
Internal Revenue Service (ruling reproduced in Appendix A)

Revenue Ruling 59-60 supplies the federal tax framework for valuing closely held stock when no active market quotation exists. Fair market value is the price at which property would change hands between a hypothetical willing buyer and willing seller, neither under compulsion and both reasonably informed. The inquiry considers the nature and history of the business, economic and industry outlook, book value, earning capacity, dividend capacity, goodwill and other intangibles, prior stock sales, and comparable-company market data.

The ruling cautions against mechanical formulas and requires judgment based on the facts. Its hypothetical-buyer premise is a fair-market-value concept, not a definition of statutory fair value in an appraisal or oppression remedy. It therefore provides useful valuation vocabulary but does not itself decide whether a particular state's fair-value statute includes buyer-specific synergies or shareholder-level discounts.

Verition Partners Master Fund Ltd. v. Aruba Networks, Inc.

On the record presented, the Court of Chancery abused its discretion by using Aruba's unaffected thirty-day trading price. Fair value was the arm's-length deal price minus the portion attributable to merger synergies.

Hewlett-Packard acquired Aruba after an arm's-length process. In the appraisal proceeding, the Court of Chancery selected Aruba's unaffected thirty-day average market price, which was below both the deal price and the parties' valuation evidence. The Delaware Supreme Court reversed, concluding that the chosen market-price metric lacked adequate record support and that the deal process provided persuasive evidence of value.

The Court directed entry of judgment at $19.10 per share—the deal price less the value attributed to synergies. *Verition* therefore shows that an actual strategic transaction can be the best valuation evidence while preserving section 262's exclusion of buyer-created value. It supports using the market transaction as a starting point, not treating the strategic buyer's full investment value as statutory fair value.

N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7 — Involuntary Dissolution and Alternative Remedies

In qualifying closely held corporations, the court may grant dissolution or alternative equitable relief for deadlock, illegality, fraud, abuse, waste, or oppression, including an order that the corporation or other shareholders purchase a shareholder's stock at fair value.

Section 14A:12-7 authorizes judicial intervention in specified disputes involving New Jersey corporations. For corporations with twenty-five or fewer shareholders, the statutory grounds include fraudulent or illegal conduct, abuse of authority, waste or misapplication of corporate assets, and conduct that is oppressive or unfair toward one or more minority shareholders in their capacity as shareholders, directors, officers, or employees.

Subsection (8) allows the court, upon a party's motion, to order the corporation or one or more shareholders to purchase another shareholder's stock at fair value. The presumptive valuation date is the commencement of the action, although the court may select another date or make equitable adjustments where oppression caused or threatened a material change in value. The statute creates an equitable remedy; the cases determine how fair value and discounts operate on particular facts.
